html:
The ancestors of the Tai-speaking peoples, shown on the map across much of southern China in 2000 and 200 BCE. The label is broad: the area it covers also held many other peoples, including the Yue.

The Tai languages belong to the Kra-Dai family, which linguists trace to southern China, around Guangxi, Guangdong and the island of Hainan. Its early speakers were rice farmers of the river valleys, living in stilt houses, with water buffalo and boats. Chinese records count them among the southern peoples outside Chinese rule.

Over the first millennium CE, and faster after about 1000, Tai groups moved southwest along the river valleys into what are now Laos, Thailand, Myanmar and northeast India. They built the upland Thai kingdoms and later Sukhothai and Ayutthaya, forerunners of Siam. Those who stayed behind include the Zhuang, now the largest minority people of China. The map also shows Proto-Thai cultures in 400 BCE.
